INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE
Massachusetts, California, Colorado, Delaware, the
District of Columbia , Hawai‘i, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New
Mexico, New York, Oregon , Rhode Island , and Vermont respectfully submit this brief as amici curiae in
support of respondents.  Given their obligation to protect the safety and welfare of minors and their duty to
honor the fundamental rights of parents and families,
amici have a strong interest in the substantive questions underlying this lawsuit.  M ore immediately,
amici also have a vested interest in the jurisdictional
question now pending before the Court.  As amici will
explain, any erosion of the standing requirements enshrined in Article III would have a direct effect on amici in their capacity as sovereigns.
INTRODUCTION AND
SUMMARY OF THE ARGUMENT
This is—or at least should be—a case about mundane standing principles .  Petitioners earnestly oppose several Washington laws that govern what happens when a minor seeking gender-affirming care arrives at a homeless shelter in that state.  But earnest
opposition to a government  policy has never been
enough to create a  justiciable case or controversy ; to
sue in federal court, a plaintiff must point to an injury
that is “concrete and particularized”  and “actual or
imminent.”  Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S.
555, 560 (1992).  Applying well-worn standing principles, the court below held that p etitioners failed to
make these threshold showings.
Petitioners and their amici now treat those wellworn principles as an afterthought, urging this Court
instead to recognize two new pathways to Article III

2

standing.  Petitioners first propose an aggressive “object-of-the-law” test,  under which any  person who
claims to be “targeted” by a law —including someone
who face s no imminent, real -world injury—would
have standing to bring a legal challenge.  As a fall -
back, petitioners suggest—and the United States expressly argues—that parental-rights claims are so exceptional that they warrant their own loosened standing requirements.  The upshot of these novel theories:
on petitioners’ view, even parents who do “not .  . .
ha[ve] a gender -dysphoric child”  (Br. 27) may  challenge a policy that concerns minors’ access to genderaffirming care.
The Court should reject that proposed dilution of
the injury -in-fact requirement .  As respondents explain at greater length, petitioners’ arguments are inconsistent with blackletter standing principles, which
are sufficient to resolve this case  in respondents’ favor.  This brief underscores an additional point: adopting petitioners’ proffered tests would be a practical
nightmare.  Amici routinely enact laws to protect the
welfare of minors , i ncluding law s about custody,
guardianship, child support, schooling, youth employment, immunization, vehicle safety , and a host of
other topics.  As amici can attest, the existing injury -
in-fact framework leaves no shortage of plaintiffs with
standing to challenge these laws.  That is as it should
be: state governments expect to defend their actions
in federal court against timely claims brought by parties with a concrete stake in the outcome.  But petitioners’ approach would go further , subjecting state
statutes and regulations to claims by individuals
without such a concrete stake.  T he federal courts
should not be in the business of refereeing academic
disputes, and the states should not have to expend
their already scarce resources to litigate them.   T he

3

Court should decline petitioners’ invitation to rethink
standing law and should affirm the judgment below.
ARGUMENT
A. Ordinary standing principles resolve this case
in favor of respondents.
Article III , this Court has explained, requires a
plaintiff-by-plaintiff and claim -by-claim analysis of
standing.  Lujan, 547 U.S. at 352.  In a given parentalrights case, therefore, the parties  can naturally have
good-faith disagreements over whether  specific parents have established concrete and imminent injuries
on the facts alleged.  What should not be up for debate,
however, is whether a court will resolve th e question
of injury using the same settled principles that govern
every other case.  Those principles readily defeat petitioners’ claim that the mere existence of Washington’s
law causes them a concrete injury in fact.
1.  This Court hardly needs reminding of its established framework for evaluating standing.  To satisfy
Article III, a plaintiff “must have (1) suffered an injury
in fact, (2) that is fairly traceable to the challenged
conduct of the defendant, and (3) that is likely to be
redressed by a favorable judicial decision.”  Spokeo,
Inc. v. Robins, 578 U.S. 330, 338 (2016) .  The “foremost” of these elements —injury in fact—in turn requires a plaintiff to establish a “concrete and particularized” invasion of a legally protected interest that
is “actual or imminent, not conjectural or hypothetical.”  Id. at 338-339 (quotation marks omitted).  These
standing requirements stem from the text of  Article
III, which limits federal-court jurisdiction to discrete
“Cases” and “Controversies.”  Together, they preserve
the separation of powers; prevent courts from issuing
advisory opinions; and ensure that lawsuits involve

4

genuine, adversarial disputes rather than abstract or
generalized grievances.  See Clapper v. Amnesty Int’l
USA, 568 U.S. 398, 408-409 (2013).
2.  The same well-worn principles suffice to resolve
this case.  Like every other federal-court plaintiff, petitioners must show that they are experiencing a “concrete and particularized” invasion of a legally protected interest that is “actual or imminent, not conjectural or hypothetical.”  Spokeo , 578 U.S. at 338.  To
determine whether petitioners have carried that burden, a court must consider a host of case-specific facts,
including, among other things, whether each plaintiff
has a child who is likely to seek gender-affirming care;
whether that child is likely to run away  at all ; and
whether that child is likely to run away to a licensed
homeless shelter covered by the challenged laws (e.g.,
because the child is aware of those laws and their implications).  See Resp. Br. 42.  As the district court and
court of appeals found, that familiar inquiry is where
this case begins and ends.  See, e.g. , Pet. App. 21a
(holding that certain parents lacked standing because
they offered “no allegation that [ their child] is transgender, has sought gender -affirming treatment, or
has expressed an interest in running away”).
B. Petitioners’ new theories of Article III injury
are legally and practically unsound.
Perhaps recognizing they have not made the showings necessary to  survive a traditional standing inquiry, petitioners and their amici advance two other
theories of Article III  injury.  Neither is consistent
with settled law, and both would create  problems in
practice.

5

1. The Court should reject petitioners’ amorphous object-of-the-law test.
Petitioners first argue (Br. 21 -31) that they have
standing because they are the “objects” or “targets” of
the challenged statutes.   That argument breaks with
settled precedent; lacks internal consistency; and, if
adopted, would expose state and local governments to
a flood of new litigation raising abstract questions.
a.  Although petitioners try to situate their objectof-the-law test within existing doctrine, it looks nothing like any view of injury this Court has previously
adopted.  Relying largely on the floor statements of individual legislators (see Pet. Br. 25), petitioners argue
that the challenged Washington statutes target parents who oppose gender-affirming care, and that every
such parent therefore has standing to sue.  According
to petitioners (Br. 34-35), the only thing their objectof-the-law test requires is that a parent (1) “oppose
gender transitioning” and (2) “have a minor capable of
understanding gender and running away.”   In other
words, petitioners’ test would confer standing on parents whose children do not identify as transgender or
have gender dysphoria, as well as parents whose children, although capable in theory of running away to a
Washington homeless shelter , have no likelihood  of
ever doing so.  See Pet. Br. 27 (arguing that a parent
is an object of the law “whether or not the parent has
a gender-dysphoric child”).
Precedent forecloses t hat sweeping theory of injury.  As the Court has repeatedly (and recently) admonished, mere disagreement with government action—even deeply held, good -faith disagreement —
does not qualify as a n Article III injury.  See FDA v.
Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine, 602 U.S. 367, 390
n. 3 (2024)  (“[D]istress at or disagreement with the

6

activities of others is not a basis under Article III for
a plaintiff to bring a federal lawsuit challenging the
legality of a government regulation allowing those activities.”).  Instead, would-be plaintiffs must show that
a challenged government action has had some realworld effect on them.  See supra, at 3-4.  Such a realworld effect, the Court has made clear, is part of “the
irreducible constitutional minimum of standing.”  Lujan, 504 U.S. at 560.
Petitioners’ authorities do not support their arguments to the contrary.  Petitioners rely heavily on the
emergency-docket decision in Mirabelli  v. Bonta, 607
U.S. 492 (2026), but each and every named parent in
that case had alleged that the challenged school policies actually deprived them of requested information
after their children actually “socially transitioned” at
school.  See id. at 492-494; see also Emergency Appl.
at 11-13, 58a-60a, Mirabelli v. Bonta, No. 25A810
(Jan. 8, 2025) (discussing the Doe and Poe parents). 1
Petitioners also emphasize  the decision in  Diamond
Alternative Energy, LLC v. EPA, 606 U.S. 100 (2025),
but that case merely explained  that when a law directly regulates party A and has a n immediate and
predictable real-world effect on party B, party B “might
be” an object of the law.  Id. at 115 (“If the government

1 Petitioners suggest (Br. 26) that Mirabelli “conferred standing on absent class members” whose injuries were more speculative than those of the named plaintiffs in that case.  Even accepting petitioners’ characterization of the Court’s decision, however,
the injunction in Mirabelli only reached objecting parents whose
children attended the public schools where the challenged policies were in force.  See Emergency Appl. at 80a, Mirabelli, supra.
Here, by contrast, petitioners’ theory would extend standing to
objecting parents who cannot show that their children have any
likelihood of ever finding themselves in the licensed homeless
shelters where the challenged policies are in force.

7

prohibits aluminum bats in Little League, then aluminum bat manufacturers, not only Little League,
might be objects of the regulation.”).
Neither of these decisions comes close to endorsing
petitioners’ extreme understanding of what it means
to be an “object” of a law.  Again, petitioners maintain
that parents have standing even if their children have
no reasonable prospect of ever running away to a
Washington homeless shelter  while seeking genderaffirming care.  That account of Article III strays far
beyond the boundaries of existing law.
b.  Petitioners’ theory is also internally inconsistent, with arbitrary lines separating the parents it
covers from those it does not.  For example, petitioners
insist (Br. 27) that a parent is an object of the challenged Washington laws “whether or not the parent
has a gender-dysphoric child.”  In an effort to demonstrate that their injuries are particularized, however,
petitioners simultaneously contend that parents whose
children are too young to run away would not be objects of the challenged laws.  According to petitioners,
the latter parents “ha[ve] no reason to alter their parenting now”; the challenged laws “ha[ve] not changed
these [parents’] legal status”  until their children are
old enough to run away.   Pet. Br. 34 n. 16 (emphasis
added).  But that logic applies equally to parents whose
children do not have (and have never exhibited) signs
of gender dysphoria : those parents, too, have no reason to alter their parenting now , and the law has not
changed their legal status.
The fact that petitioners’ test would confer standing on one set of parents (those whose children exhibit
no signs of gender dysphoria) but not the other (those
whose children are too young  to run away)  demonstrates its fundamental incoherence.  Such a  results-

8

oriented test is not capable of principled application.
c.  Finally, even setting aside the deficiencies just
described, petitioners’ test would cause problems in
practice.  Every day, state governments address countless public-policy debates through the legislative process, resulting in laws with numerous putative “targets” or “objects.”  This year alone, for example, state
legislatures have enacted at least 700 bills on primary
and secondary education, at least 250 bills on artificial
intelligence, at least 200 bills on immigration, and at
least 450 bills on policing and law enforcement.2  And
those are just four particularly high-profile topics: collectively, the states enact tens of thousands of new
laws each year.3  Petitioners’ amorphous object-of-thelaw test would grant Article III standing to any individual or organization who could plausibly claim to be
“targeted” by any one of these laws—even if the challenged law would never realistically affect the plaintiff in question.

(all websites last visited Oct. 28, 2026).  For purposes of this discussion, the term “state legislatures” includes the legislatures of
the District of Columbia and U.S. territories.

9

The result would be a flood of new federal litigation
raising abstract disputes.  Federal lawsuits challenging state statutes and regulations already consume a
significant amount of public resources —both for the
state and local governments that must defend against
those lawsuits and for the federal courts that must adjudicate them.  In our constitutional system, this use
of taxpayer money is worth it to vindicate the People’s
right to hold their governments to account.  But Article III  supplies an important check, ensuring that
these public expenditures only arise when someone
has a genuine, real-world stake in the outcome.  If this
Court erodes that check—as petitioners ask the Court
to do—state governments and lower federal courts
will need to stretch already scarce resources to handle
purely theoretical disputes.
In addition to a general increase in the number of
federal lawsuits, petitioners’ object-of-the-law test
would also have perverse consequences within the resulting lawsuits.  A case filed by a plaintiff without a
concrete stake in a challenged law is more likely than
a case filed by a proper Article III plaintiff to feature
disagreements that are antecedent to—but distinct
from—the merits.  Here, for example, petitioners and
respondents often disagree about what the challenged
Washington laws even do.  See Resp. Br. 22-23.  These
kinds of distracting disputes—which ultimately frustrate review of the merits—are far less likely to arise
in a case brought by plaintiffs who are currently facing, or imminently will face , the real-world effects of
the laws they challenge.
Moreover, because petitioners’ test requires courts
to ask whether a plaintiff is the true “object” of a law,
the test improperly invites would-be plaintiffs to cite
extratextual evidence of statutory meaning and to

10

delve into the supposed motives of individual legislators.  Petitioners’ own brief proves the point : they repeatedly rely (e.g., at 10-12, 15, 25) on the floor statements of individual Washington legislators to substantiate their claim that they are the “targets” of the
challenged laws.  See also, e.g., U.S. Amicus Br. 7 (relying on these floor statements); Florida et al. Amicus
Br. 16 (same).  Indeed, this legislative history appears
to be petitioners’ only evidence to support their claim
of targeting, given that the text of the challenged laws
treats so-called “affirming” and “non -affirming” parents the same.   See Pet. Br. 30 (conceding that the
challenged laws apply to “the child of ‘affirming’ parents who currently receives or seeks ‘gender-affirming
treatment’ upon running away”).   This Court is typically reluctant to inquire into the supposed motives
of individual legislators.  See, e.g. , Dobbs v. Jackson
Women’s Health Org., 597 U.S. 215, 253- 254 (2022);
United States v. O’Brien, 391 U.S. 367, 383-384 (1968).
So are state  courts.  See, e.g., Administrative Justice
of the Housing Ct. Dep ’t v. Comm’r of Admin ., 391
Mass. 198, 205 (1984); Grupe Dev. Co. v. Superior Ct.,
4 Cal. 4th 911, 922 (1993).  An approach that calls for
that kind of inquiry should raise red flags.
2. The Court should not c reate a parentalrights exception to the usual  standing
rules.
In addition to their object-of-the-law theory, petitioners also appear to ask the Court to  create a new
exception to ordinary standing rules for cases involving parents’ fundamental right to direct the upbringing of their children.  See Pet. Br. 23 (arguing that petitioners’ relaxed theory of injury  “is particularly apt
as to parental rights”).  The United States advances a
more full -throated version of  that request, seeking

11

such an exception even as it admits ( Amicus Br. 21)
that petitioners’ other arguments “extend far too
broadly.”  Under this novel standing theory, a statute
that allegedly affects any parent-child relationship
causes a per se “injury” to all parents by operation of
the law alone.  See U.S. Amicus Br. 17 (arguing that a
parent “suffer[s] an Article III  injury when the government changes a fundamental aspect of the parentchild relationship —not just when a child takes advantage of that new relationship [] and acts against
their parents’ wishes”).  Like petitioners’ object-of-thelaw test, however, this parental-rights exception is legally, logically, and practically unsound.
a.  Doctrinally, the United States bases  its argument for a parental -rights exception on the premise
that the right to direct the upbringing of one’s children
is unique among constitutional rights.  See, e.g., U.S.
Amicus Br. 15, 17 (arguing that “parental rights occupy a special place in this Court’s precedent ,” and
that “this Court has treated parental rights as distinct
within ‘our constitutional system’”).  According to the
United States (Amicus Br. 21), because parents have
“an enforceable interest in the integrity of the parentchild relationship itself,” any law or policy touching on
that relationship automatically confers standing.  But
that theory is flawed in at least two ways.
First, it blurs the constitutional line between
rights and injuries.  No party to this case disputes that
the Constitution protects parents’ fundamental right
to make decisions con cerning the care, custody, and
control of their children.  See, e.g., Meyer v. Nebraska,
262 U.S. 390, 399 (1923) ; Pierce v. Society of the Sisters of the Holy Names of Jesus & Mary, 268 U.S. 510,
534-536 (1925).  But the fact that every parent enjoys
this fundamental right does not mean that every

12

parent has “a special license  to roam the country ”
challenging every alleged infringement of that right.
Valley Forge Christian Coll . v. Americans United for
Separation of Church & State, Inc., 454 U.S. 464, 487
(1982).
Second, the proposed parental-rights exception improperly distinguishes among  constitutional rights.
Petitioners and the United States “offer [no] sound
reason to prefer one constitutional guarantee over another” in this co ntext.  Kennedy v. Bremerton Sch .
Dist., 597 U.S. 507, 542- 543 (2022).  They fail to explain, for example,  why a plaintiff invoking her fundamental parental rights should have easier access to
the federal courts than a plaintiff invoking her right
to vote, to petition the government, or  to bear arms .
Nor could plaintiffs explain that disparity: a theory of
parental-rights exceptionalism sits uneasily with the
text of the Constitution as a whole (which does not
enumerate parental rights) and of Article III specifically (which speaks of “Cases” and “Controversies”
without distinguishing among different claims).
b.  In addition to these doctrinal issues, several
other considerations militate against reading a new
parental-rights exception into Article III.
First, the proposed parental -rights exception
raises federalism and separation-of-powers concerns.
“By limiting who can sue, the standing requirement
implements the Framers’ concept of the proper —and
properly limited—role of the courts in a democratic society.”  FDA, 602 U.S. at 380 (quotation marks omitted).  Under our Constitution, “the federal courts decide some contested legal questions later rather than
sooner, thereby allowing issues to percolate and potentially be resolved by the political branches in the
democratic process. ”  Id.  (noting that “ the standing

13

requirement means that the federal courts may never
need to decide some contested legal questions”).  Consistent with these principles , parents, like all other
members of the public , must first make their policy
objections known to their elected representatives, who
may well resolve their concerns  without litigation.
And if they subsequently bring their policy disputes to
federal court, parents , like a ll other litigant s, must
show injury -in-fact—as this Court has exhaustively
defined the concept.
Second, the proposed parental -rights exception
weakens states’ own compelling interest in safeguarding the physical and mental well -being of children
within their borders.  See Globe Newspaper Co. v. Superior Ct., 457 U.S. 596, 607 (1982) ; United States v.
Skrmetti, 605 U.S. 495, 524-525 (2025).  As this Court
has explained, parents do not “have absolute and unreviewable discretion” to make medical decisions for
their children ; states also have some constitutional
discretion “in dealing with children when their physical or mental health is jeopardized.”  Parham v. J.R.,
442 U.S. 584, 603-604 (1979).  The threat of constant
litigation will likely undermine those important state
interests, frustrating states’ ability to enact and enforce laws that protect children’s privacy and safety.
Third, an automatic standing rule for parental -
rights cases will burden states and their officials with
an influx of costly litigation.  See supra, at 8-9.  In the
school context, this influx will have a chilling effect on
educators, deterring them from all manner of curricular and counseling decisions for fear that even parents
whose children are unaffected by those decisions  will
now have standing to sue.  To date, c ourts have rejected such lawsuits where parents have not alleged
an actual or imminent injury.  See, e.g., John & Jane

14

Parents 1 v. Montgomery County Bd. of Ed., 78 F.4th
622, 629-631 (4th Cir. 2023) , cert. denied, 144 S. Ct.
2560 (2024) (holding that parents lacked standing to
challenge a school board’s “Gender Identity Guidelines” because they failed to allege that “any of their
children ha[d] gender support plans”; “that their children ha[d] had any discussions with school officials
about gender-identity or gender-transition issues”; or
that they “suspect[ed] their children might be considering gender transition or have a heightened risk of
doing so ”); Parents Protecting Our Children, UA v.
Eau Claire Area Sch. Dist., 95 F.4th 501, 505 (7th Cir.
2024), cert. denied, 145 S. Ct. 14 (2024) ( holding that
a plaintiff association lacked standing because it
failed to “allege that even one of the association’s
members—any particular parent —ha[d] experienced
an actual or imminent injury attributable to [the challenged poli cies]”).  But under p etitioners’ and the
United States’ view, these and other similarly abstract lawsuits (including, potentially, lawsuits
brought by parents whose children do not even attend
a school where challenged policies are in force) will
now go forward.
And lawsuits about school policies on gender identity will not be the final frontier: states will feel the
consequences of expanded standing far beyond today’s
debates about transgender students and athletes.  So
many of the decisions that states make, in the school
context and otherwise, affect the lives of children and
families.  If the Court adopts the automatic standing
rule that petition ers and their amici advance , those
decisions will be subject to litigation by every objecting parent—even before injury or enforcement.
CONCLUSION
The Court should affirm the judgment below.

15
